title: Human Computer Interaction
body:
COMP 3553 covers the part of a system a person actually touches. Every other COMP course
measures software against the machine: is it correct, is it fast, does it scale. This one
measures it against a person, and a program that is correct, fast and unusable has failed at
the only thing it was built for.

The central claim is that usability is a property to be designed and measured, and that a
disagreement about it is settled with evidence. Human beings have specific and well-documented
limits on memory, attention and perception, and an interface either respects them or generates
errors. When a user makes a mistake, the design is the first suspect.

The course runs the full cycle: find out who the user is and what they are trying to do, build
something cheap enough to throw away, test it on people who were not involved in building it,
and repeat. That cycle is [[INTRODUCTION TO SOFTWARE ENGINEERING]]'s process
applied to the interface, with the requirements gathered by observation, since an interview
alone misses what people actually do.

## Topics

### Designing for the user

[[User-Centred Design]] puts the person's goals at the centre of every decision, and its
practical content is a warning: the designer is not the user. A developer knows the system's
model, has seen every state, and has forgotten what it was like to not know. Anything obvious
to them is evidence about them and not about anybody else.

The alternative it replaces is design driven by the implementation, where the interface exposes
whatever structure the database happens to have, and the user is required to learn it.

[[Human Capabilities]] supplies the constraints the design has to respect. Short-term
memory holds a small number of items, so an interface requiring a user to carry information
between screens will produce errors. Attention is a single resource, so an animation competing
with a form wins. Perception varies, and roughly one man in twelve has a colour vision
deficiency, so colour alone can never carry meaning.

### How an object communicates its use

[[Affordance]] is what an object makes possible: a handle affords pulling, a flat plate affords
pushing. [[Signifier]] is the perceivable indication of that possibility, which is what the
user actually sees. A door with a handle on the push side affords pushing and signifies
pulling, which is why people collide with it, and that mismatch is the standard example of the
whole topic.

[[Interface Metaphor]] borrows structure from something the user already understands,
which is why files sit in folders on a desktop. The borrowed structure carries expectations,
and where the software departs from the metaphor the user is misled by exactly the thing that
was meant to help.

[[Skeuomorphism]] is the strongest form, imitating a physical object's appearance. A save icon
shaped like a floppy disk survives long after the object it depicts, and it works now as a
learned symbol, and the metaphor it started as has stopped mattering, which is what happens to
every metaphor eventually. Flat design abandons the imitation and keeps the signifiers, and it
fails when it removes so much visual difference that a button stops looking clickable.

### Preventing and surviving errors

[[Feedback]] is the system's response confirming that something happened. Its absence is what
produces the repeated click, because a user with no confirmation assumes the action was lost.
The required speed is set by human perception, and engineering convenience has no say in it:
response within about a tenth of a second feels instantaneous, a second holds the user's flow
of thought, and ten seconds loses their attention entirely, so anything slower needs a progress
indicator to keep the user informed.

[[Consistency and Standards]] is why a design should follow platform conventions,
even where a better one could be invented. A user arrives having learned every other
application, and that learning transfers only when the new interface behaves the same way. A
genuinely better control that behaves differently costs every user the relearning, and the
improvement rarely pays for it.

Error handling divides into preventing the error and supporting recovery. Prevention means
making the wrong action impossible, by disabling what cannot be selected and by constraining
input to valid values. Recovery means undo, since a user who knows an action is reversible
explores freely and one who does not proceeds slowly and asks for help.

### The design cycle

[[User Persona]] is a concrete description of a representative user, built from research,
with a name, a goal and a level of expertise. Its function is to stop the abstract user, who
has no constraints and adapts to anything, from being the person the team designs for.

[[Task Analysis]] describes what the user is trying to accomplish, broken into steps, and
it is what reveals that a task the software treats as one operation is five to the person, or
that two screens are always used together. The design follows the task, so the analysis comes
first.

[[Prototyping]] builds something to test, and the result is thrown away. Low fidelity means
paper sketches and [[Wireframe|wireframes]], which cost minutes and get discarded without
regret, and that disposability is the point: a prototype somebody spent a week on will be
defended in a meeting. High fidelity means an interactive mockup that behaves enough to be
used, and it is built once the layout questions are settled.

Implementation then applies ordinary software skills to the interface, and
[[WEB DEVELOPMENT FOR CS]] supplies the mechanisms, since a form's structure,
its labels and its validation messages are all interface decisions expressed in [[HTML]] and
the [[DOM]].

### Evaluating an interface

Three methods, ordered by cost and by what each catches.

[[Heuristic Evaluation]] has evaluators inspect the interface against a checklist, and
[[Nielsen's Heuristics]] is the standard list of ten. It is cheap, needs no users, and
finds a large fraction of problems, and it misses anything that depends on what a real user is
trying to do.

[[Cognitive Walkthrough]] steps through a specific task one action at a time, asking at
each step whether the user would know what to do and whether they would see that it worked. It
is aimed at first-time use and catches problems in learnability specifically.

[[Usability Testing]] puts real users in front of the system with real tasks and observes.
It is the only method that produces evidence about behaviour, where the others produce expert
judgement, and its results are quantitative: task completion rate, time on task, error count,
and where people got stuck. The discipline is to give the task and then stay silent, since a
tester who explains has destroyed the measurement.

### Accessibility and impact

[[Accessibility]] is design that works for users with disabilities, and the course treats it as
a requirement of a correct interface. Its practical content is specific: every image needs a
text alternative, colour can never be the only carrier of meaning, everything reachable by
mouse must be reachable by keyboard, and contrast has to meet a measurable ratio.

The general case is that accessible design is better design for everyone. Captions serve a
noisy room, keyboard access serves a power user, and clear contrast serves a phone in sunlight,
which is why the constraint improves the product and pays for itself.

The socio-organisational block closes the course by asking what happens when a system is
deployed into an organisation, where a tool that changes a workflow changes who holds
information and who is accountable, and those effects are what
[[INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY AND SOCIETY]] examines.

## Related courses

- [[INTRODUCTION TO SOFTWARE ENGINEERING]] (COMP 2633) supplies the process this course
  applies to the interface, where [[Use Case Diagrams]] describe the system from the outside
  and [[Software Requirements Analysis]] is [[Task Analysis]] at the level of the whole
  system.
- [[WEB DEVELOPMENT FOR CS]] (COMP 3612) is where the interface gets built, in [[HTML]], the
  [[Form Tag]], the [[DOM]] and [[Event Handling]], and where [[DOM Performance]] decides
  whether the [[Feedback]] arrives inside the time a user tolerates.
- [[INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY AND SOCIETY]] (COMP 3309) evaluates the same design decisions
  ethically, since an interface shapes what a user understands they are agreeing to, which is
  the consent question in [[Data Privacy]].
- [[STATISTICS]] (MATH 2234) supplies the analysis behind [[Usability Testing]], since a
  difference in task time between two designs is a claim needing [[Hypothesis Testing]] and a
  [[Sampling Distribution]] to support it.
- [[ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE]] and [[MACHINE LEARNING]] produce systems whose behaviour is
  probabilistic, which makes [[Feedback]] harder to design, since the interface has to
  communicate confidence alongside the result.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE]] (COMP 1631) has [[Errors]], and the distinction between
  an error the system reports and an error the user cannot recover from is where this course
  starts.
